stem: What best describes an AI Center of Excellence?

options.text: A cross-functional group that sets standards and supports AI delivery
A single data science team that builds every model itself
An outside body that certifies finished AI products for sale
A help desk that answers staff questions about software invoices

explanation: A Center of Excellence is an internal cross-functional group that defines standards and supports AI work across the business. One data science team lacks the security and engineering mix, an outside certifier is not internal, and a help desk handles support requests rather than governance.

stem: Three business units at Harbor Quill Insurance each bought a different summarization tool and wrote their own review checklist. Which governance structure best fixes the duplication?

options.text: A larger purchasing budget so every business unit can buy its own tool
A central team that curates tools and sets shared standards
A yearly survey asking each unit which tool it likes
A ban on summarization tools across the whole company

explanation: A central AI Center of Excellence curates tools and defines standards, so units stop duplicating choices and risk work. More budget would multiply the duplication, a survey records preferences without deciding anything, and a ban removes the business benefit instead of governing it.

stem: An engineering team asks why it must complete a shared evaluation template before launching a chatbot when its own tests already passed. Which answer from the Center of Excellence is best?

options.text: It replaces the team's own testing with central testing
It lets the central group take ownership of the chatbot afterward
It sets one bar that every launch is judged against
It ranks teams by how quickly they deliver

explanation: The Center of Excellence defines standards and reviews projects, so a common template holds every launch to one bar. It does not replace the team's testing, transfer ownership of the chatbot, or score delivery speed.

stem: A new Center of Excellence staffed only with data scientists and machine learning engineers shipped a chatbot that revealed its hidden instructions to the first tester. Which skill set was missing from the group?

options.text: Vendor contract negotiation expertise
Front-end design and user research
Payroll and benefits administration
Information security expertise

explanation: The leak is a security failure, and a Center of Excellence needs security expertise alongside engineering and data science. Contract negotiation, interface design and payroll are useful business skills but would not have caught the exposure.

stem: Which statement correctly separates an AI policy from an AI procedure?

options.text: A policy lists click-by-click steps and a procedure states general intent
A policy binds only vendors and a procedure binds only employees
A policy sets rules and authority and a procedure details who does what
A policy is optional advice and a procedure is a regulation

explanation: A policy defines what is allowed and who decides, while a procedure converts that policy into predictable steps with owners and evidence. The first option swaps the two, neither document is limited to a single audience, and a policy is a mandatory internal rule rather than optional advice.

stem: A document at Brightmoor Credit forbids entering customer PII into external generative AI services and lists who may grant exemptions. What kind of governance document is this?

options.text: An AI procedure with numbered steps for requesting an exemption
An AI policy that sets a data-use rule and names approvers
A technical guardrail that blocks sensitive fields from leaving
An audit report listing the exemptions granted last quarter

explanation: A rule plus a named decision authority is the content of an AI policy. A procedure would list steps and evidence, a guardrail is a tooling control that enforces the rule, and an audit report records findings after the fact.

stem: A document tells staff: open a ticket in the model registry, attach the data owner sign-off, and have the reviewer record the decision against the ticket. Which description fits it best?

options.text: An AI policy stating the boundaries of acceptable use
A risk register entry that scores the exposure of one AI use case
An audit finding about a missed approval step
An AI procedure assigning role-based steps and evidence

explanation: Numbered, role-based steps with evidence are what an AI procedure provides, making decisions traceable. A policy gives boundaries instead of workflow, a risk register entry rates one use case, and an audit finding reports a gap rather than prescribing steps.

stem: Which event most justifies revising an AI policy ahead of its normal review date?

options.text: The business starts a type of AI use that the wording does not cover
A team finishes a routine retraining run of an existing production model
A vendor publishes a newsletter about upcoming model releases
The office changes its seating plan for the next quarter

explanation: A new kind of AI use falls outside the existing rules, so the policy needs updating to give authority and boundaries for it. Routine retraining is handled by procedure, and newsletters or seating changes do not alter what the organization permits.

stem: A clause in an AI policy requires that a named person can override a model's recommendation on job applicants. What does this clause mainly address?

options.text: Protection of personal data in training sets
Human oversight of automated decisions
Recovery of the service after an outage
Retirement of outdated model versions

explanation: Letting a person override an automated recommendation is human oversight. Data protection concerns what data is collected and used, recovery concerns availability, and retirement concerns the end of a model's life cycle.

stem: Which feature makes an AI procedure valuable to people who must later verify it was followed?

options.text: It is worded in careful legal language to prevent disputes
It keeps steps broad so teams can interpret them freely
It records who acted, when, and with what evidence
It routes decisions to whichever team is free that day

explanation: Procedures turn policy into auditable actions, so naming who did what and when with evidence makes decisions traceable. Legal language and loose steps reduce clarity, and ad hoc routing removes accountability.

stem: After an incident, investigators at Pellwick Bank cannot tell who authorized a change to a prompt template or what evidence that person saw. Which governance gap does this most directly show?

options.text: An undersized training cluster for building and testing new models
Weak masking of PII in the test data
No diagram of the vector database layout
No procedure with traceable, role-based sign-off steps

explanation: Missing records of who authorized a change point to the absence of an AI procedure that assigns roles and captures evidence. Cluster size, masking and diagrams may matter elsewhere but none explains lost traceability.

stem: An AI policy says no model may touch regulated data without masking. Pipeline software now masks the fields automatically before any data reaches a model. What does this software represent?

options.text: A technical guardrail that enforces the policy
A procedure that records every approval and its reviewer
A second policy that overlaps the first
An audit that tests masking afterward

explanation: Guardrails are controls that enforce governance in daily operations, and automatic masking applies the policy rule without relying on people. It is not a procedure of recorded steps, not a new policy document, and not an audit, which checks results after the fact.

stem: A security analyst gets an alert that a customer-facing model may have been poisoned. Which document should she follow to learn who to call and which records to keep?

options.text: The purpose and scope section of the AI policy
The Center of Excellence charter and its member list
A vendor datasheet describing the model's tested accuracy
An incident procedure naming roles and evidence steps

explanation: A procedure translates policy into role-based steps, including who acts and what evidence is kept during an incident. The policy scope states what is covered, the charter describes the group, and a datasheet says nothing about how to respond.

stem: A nightly feed of store sales arrives two hours late, and a vendor renamed a column without notice, breaking the loads. Which role should rework the ingestion jobs?

options.text: Data scientist
AI risk analyst
Data engineer
AI auditor

explanation: Data engineers build and maintain the pipelines that deliver data, so ingestion failures are theirs to fix. A data scientist consumes the data, a risk analyst rates use cases, and an auditor provides independent assurance.

stem: A retailer wants proof that past purchase history can predict which items get returned. Which role would test which customer attributes carry signal and produce a simple first model?

options.text: Data scientist
ML engineer
Platform engineer
AI architect

explanation: Testing which attributes carry signal and building a simple first model is data scientist work. The ML engineer later readies a model for production, the platform engineer supplies infrastructure, and the architect designs how components fit together.

stem: At a hand-off meeting, researchers present a fraud model that only runs in a notebook on one laptop. Which role takes it and makes it ready to serve real traffic reliably?

options.text: Data scientist
AI risk analyst
Data engineer
ML engineer

explanation: Preparing a prototype for dependable production use is machine learning engineer work. The data scientist produced the prototype, the risk analyst rates exposure, and the data engineer feeds data rather than reworking model code.

stem: A hospital wants a triage assistant that connects to its scheduling and records systems. Before any coding, which role produces the design showing how the assistant links to those systems and what path the data takes?

options.text: ML engineer
AI architect
MLOps engineer
AI auditor

explanation: The AI architect designs how components fit together, including data flows and integration with existing systems. The ML engineer builds the model, the MLOps engineer automates its life cycle later, and the auditor verifies rather than designs.

stem: Three squads at Orrin Logistics each built their own compute setup, and one left an experiment environment open to the internet. The fix is a single standard foundation of compute and network isolation that all squads share, not new pipelines or a new system design. Which role should provide it?

options.text: MLOps engineer
AI architect
Platform engineer
Data engineer

explanation: The platform engineer owns the shared infrastructure that teams build on. MLOps automates the model life cycle on top of it, the architect designs the overall solution, and the data engineer handles data pipelines.

stem: Six weeks after launch, a pricing model's errors creep up as markets change, and nobody is alerted. Which role should set up automated checks, a scheduled refresh and a way to revert to the previous version?

options.text: MLOps engineer
AI auditor
Data engineer
AI security architect

explanation: MLOps engineers automate the model life cycle, including monitoring for drift, retraining and rollback. Auditors verify afterward, data engineers manage data pipelines, and security architects design protections against attackers.

stem: A red team shows that a support chatbot obeys instructions hidden in pasted documents. Which role designs the defenses, such as separating untrusted text and limiting what the bot can reach?

options.text: AI governance engineer
AI risk analyst
ML engineer
AI security architect

explanation: Designing safeguards against attacks on a model's prompts and data is the AI security architect's duty. The governance engineer builds approval workflows, the risk analyst rates exposure, and the ML engineer productionizes models.

stem: Compliance requires a recorded sign-off before each model launch and evidence kept for a set period. The flows needed are approval and retention rules, not build or deployment pipelines. Which role builds them and keeps the records?

options.text: AI risk analyst
AI governance engineer
AI security architect
MLOps engineer

explanation: The AI governance engineer builds policy into everyday workflows by codifying approvals and keeping the evidence. The risk analyst rates risk, the security architect designs technical protection, and the MLOps engineer automates model delivery rather than policy obligations.

stem: A bank's innovation lab proposes a model that flags customers for extra checks. A committee meets Friday and wants a written view of the regulatory, fairness and commercial downsides with suggested safeguards. Which role prepares it?

options.text: AI auditor
AI security architect
AI risk analyst
AI governance engineer

explanation: Rating a proposed use case against risk criteria and suggesting mitigations is AI risk analyst work. The auditor gives independent assurance after the fact, the security architect designs technical protection, and the governance engineer automates approvals.

stem: After a regulator's letter, Hartwell Group's board wants someone with no stake in the delivery teams to take a handful of past launches, retrace how each decision was reached, and tell the board whether the rules were followed. Which role is this?

options.text: AI auditor
AI governance engineer
AI risk analyst
AI architect

explanation: Independent sampling and recreation of decisions is the AI auditor's role. The governance engineer operates the workflows being checked, the risk analyst assesses use cases before launch, and the architect designs systems.

stem: At Corvane Systems the engineer who designed a model gateway's access controls also reviews them each quarter and signs the report. What is the main weakness?

options.text: The engineer lacks permission to read gateway logs
A quarterly review is too slow to catch problems
Access controls need more model knowledge than designers have
The same person is checking their own earlier work

explanation: Independence matters because reviewing your own work weakens assurance, so an auditor separate from the builders should verify controls. The engineer can usually read logs, review frequency is not the issue, and model knowledge does not decide independence.

stem: Consider two job postings. One wants a person to build and attack-test the defenses around a model's endpoint; the other wants a person outside the delivery line to check that alerts and escalations happen as written. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: First is the AI auditor, second is the AI security architect
First is the AI security architect, second is the AI auditor
First is the AI governance engineer, second is the AI risk analyst
First is the MLOps engineer, second is the platform engineer

explanation: Architects design and test protections, and auditors verify independently that operations match what is documented. The first option swaps them, and the remaining pairings assign workflow, risk rating, life cycle or infrastructure duties instead.

stem: A team wants to loosen a response filter that enforces the data-use policy because it blocks too many answers. Under sound governance, who should approve the change?

options.text: The developer who noticed the problem, after testing it
Whoever is on call, through a chat message
The named authority, with a recorded decision
The model vendor, through a support ticket

explanation: A guardrail enforces policy, so changes to it need the policy authority's decision and a record. A developer or on-call person lacks that authority, and a vendor does not own the organization's rules.

stem: Which statement about a written AI policy and the technical guardrails that enforce it is accurate?

options.text: The policy states the rule and the guardrail applies it uniformly at scale across requests
The guardrail makes it unnecessary to state the rule in writing
The guardrail decides who holds approval authority for exceptions
The policy is enforced through procedure, so guardrails add no value

explanation: Policy defines the rule and authority, while guardrails apply the rule uniformly across many requests. Guardrails cannot replace written rules, do not assign authority, and add consistency that procedures run by people cannot guarantee.

stem: Which statement belongs in the purpose and scope section of an AI policy?

options.text: It names the systems, users and uses it covers
It sets the drift thresholds that trigger an alert
It gives the commands used to roll back a release
It assigns the auditors for the current quarter

explanation: Scope names what and who the policy applies to. Alert thresholds and rollback commands are operational detail for procedures and tooling, and audit assignments are scheduling matters.

stem: An executive asks who may grant a waiver of an AI rule. In which part of the governing document should that be stated?

options.text: In the testing standard for model accuracy thresholds
In the roles and accountability section, naming who decides
In the data retention schedule for training records
In a checklist item that each team words itself

explanation: Policy says who is authorized to decide, so waiver authority belongs with roles and accountability. A testing standard, a retention schedule and self-written checklist items are neither the place for decision authority nor consistent.

stem: A Center of Excellence is chartered at Redfern Bank. Which TWO activities fit its role?

options.text: Reviewing proposed AI projects against shared standards
Running overnight retraining jobs for production models
Giving the final independent opinion on control effectiveness
Maintaining a vetted catalog of approved AI tools and platforms
Writing each team's training code
Patching the servers that host AI models

explanation: A Center of Excellence reviews projects against standards and curates tools and platforms as a strategic hub. Retraining jobs belong to the team running the model life cycle, independent opinions come from auditors, and writing code or patching servers belong to delivery and platform teams.

stem: Which THREE items would normally be written into an AI policy?

options.text: Ticket steps for filing a model change request
Roles and accountability for AI decisions
Rules governing how data may be used
Screenshots showing where to click in the registry
Requirements for human oversight of AI decisions
The order in which on-call staff are paged

explanation: Policies define accountability, data use and human oversight along with scope, security, privacy and incident response. Ticket steps, click-by-click screenshots and paging order are procedure-level detail.

stem: Wexley Corp is rewriting its AI procedures. Staff say the wording is dense and nobody can tell which steps are theirs. Which TWO changes address these problems?

options.text: State general intent and let each team fill in the details
Move the text into contract-style legal clauses
Organize steps by role so each person finds their own
Leave the choice of evidence to each reviewer
Replace jargon with plain wording that staff understand

explanation: Good procedures are role-based and plain, so people can follow them and decisions stay traceable. General intent without detail describes a policy, legal drafting hinders use, and leaving evidence undefined breaks auditability.

stem: Pallan Bank engages an AI auditor who sits outside the delivery teams. Which TWO tasks fit that role?

options.text: Designing and configuring access controls for the model gateway
Pulling sample records to check that approvals matched policy
Retraining a model when monitoring shows drift has appeared
Checking that incident handling followed the written procedure
Building the first baseline model from candidate features

explanation: Auditors sample records and verify that approvals and incident handling happen as documented. Designing controls is the security architect, retraining belongs to the team running the model life cycle, and baseline models are built by data scientists.

stem: A bank wants its sign-off and record-keeping rules enforced automatically in daily tooling. Which TWO tasks belong to the AI governance engineer?

options.text: Encoding approval rules as ticket workflows
Scoring the fairness and legal exposure of a proposed use case
Designing network isolation for the inference service
Selecting features for a first baseline model
Configuring tooling so evidence is retained and checked
Orchestrating scheduled retraining jobs for models

explanation: The governance engineer builds approvals into workflows and enforces evidence retention. Exposure scoring is the risk analyst, isolation design is the security architect, feature selection is the data scientist, and retraining jobs belong to the team running the model life cycle.

stem: Which THREE statements about governing technical guardrails are sound?

options.text: A named owner approves changes to a guardrail's rules
The policy states what the guardrail must enforce
Changes to a guardrail leave an audit trail
Anyone on call may switch a guardrail off if it is noisy
Guardrails need no review once they are deployed
Teams tune guardrail thresholds privately without a record

explanation: Guardrails enforce policy, so the policy defines what they enforce, a named owner approves changes, and a trail keeps decisions traceable. Switching them off ad hoc, skipping review and tuning in private undermine the governance they are meant to support.

stem: Match each role to the one duty it owns. One duty matches no role.

choices.text: Reports findings through a line independent of delivery teams
Compares candidate algorithms on held-out data
Tracks key risk indicators and reports the trend
Tunes inference latency and packages the model for release
Offers self-service workspace templates with isolation built in
Blocks a release in the pipeline when required evidence is missing
Adds schema checks to the vendor file ingestion jobs

explanation: Each duty is distinctive: comparing algorithms is data scientist work, latency tuning and packaging the ML engineer's, workspace templates the platform engineer's, evidence-gated releases the governance engineer's, indicator tracking the risk analyst's, and independent reporting the auditor's. Schema checks on ingestion are a data engineer duty and have no matching prompt.

partExplanations.p1: Comparing candidate algorithms on held-out data is baseline modeling.
partExplanations.p2: Latency tuning and packaging make a model ready for release.
partExplanations.p3: Self-service isolated workspaces are shared infrastructure.
partExplanations.p4: Pipeline checks for required evidence are codified governance workflows.
partExplanations.p5: Tracking risk indicators over time is a risk analyst task.
partExplanations.p6: Independent reporting lines are what separate auditors from delivery teams.

stem: A company is standing up AI governance. Match each task to the structure or role that owns it.

prompts.text: Hold a monthly forum where teams present AI plans and get cross-team advice
Declare which AI uses are permitted and which are prohibited company-wide
Provide a checklist for onboarding a new dataset, with an owner and due date per step
Configure the release pipeline to refuse a launch that lacks recorded sign-off
Give the board an independent view of whether controls work

explanation: The Center of Excellence is the cross-team hub, policy sets permitted and prohibited uses, a procedure gives owned and dated steps, the governance engineer builds the sign-off gate, and the auditor gives independent assurance. The risk analyst and platform engineer own none of these tasks.

partExplanations.p1: A cross-team forum is Center of Excellence work.
partExplanations.p2: Permitted and prohibited uses are boundaries that a policy defines.
partExplanations.p3: A checklist with owners and dates is a procedure.
partExplanations.p4: Codifying an approval gate in the pipeline is the governance engineer's task.
partExplanations.p5: Independent assurance is the auditor's role.

stem: Sort each item into the governance element that produces it.

items.text: A reference architecture reviewed by engineering, data and security experts
A prohibition on using AI to profile staff covertly
A step requiring the evaluator to log name and date before sign-off
A design review verdict on a proposed project, measured against shared standards
A principle that AI outputs must be explainable to affected people
A step list for retiring an old model version

explanation: The Center of Excellence produces shared reference designs and project reviews, the policy states prohibitions and principles, and procedures give steps that make actions traceable.

partExplanations.i1: A shared reference design is a Center of Excellence product.
partExplanations.i2: A prohibition is a policy rule.
partExplanations.i3: A step that captures name and date is part of a procedure.
partExplanations.i4: Reviewing a project against shared standards is Center of Excellence work.
partExplanations.i5: A principle that governs outputs belongs in the policy.
partExplanations.i6: A step list for a task is a procedure.

stem: Marlowe Freight is standing up AI governance. Put the steps in the order they should happen, using these rules: no group acts before it has a charter; policy scope is drafted from what is already running; procedures implement a published policy; training covers the procedures as well as the policy; an audit tests practice only after staff have been trained.

steps.text: Process owners write role-based procedures that carry out the policy
An AI auditor samples records to confirm practice follows the policy
The Center of Excellence lists the AI uses already running in the company
Staff are trained on the policy and on the procedures for their roles
The sponsor approves a charter and appoints members of the AI Center of Excellence
Leadership publishes the AI policy and names who holds approval authority

explanation: A charter creates the Center of Excellence, which inventories current AI uses so the policy scope is realistic. The policy is published, procedures implement it, staff are trained on both, and only then does an auditor test practice.

partExplanations.0: The charter must exist before the Center of Excellence can act.
partExplanations.1: The inventory of existing uses shapes the policy scope.
partExplanations.2: The policy sets authority and boundaries once scope is known.
partExplanations.4: Training covers the procedures, so it follows them.
partExplanations.5: The audit comes last because it tests how trained staff actually work.

stem: Kestrel Health delivers a machine learning model through the stages shown, ordered by each role's main hand-off. Place the role that owns the output of each stage.
explanation: The data engineer owns the feed, the platform engineer the workspace, the data scientist the prototype, the ML engineer the release package, MLOps the refresh and revert plan, and the security architect the protected inference endpoint. The auditor verifies independently and owns no stage.

partExplanations.z1: The data engineer owns the data feed.
partExplanations.z2: Isolated workspaces are shared infrastructure from the platform engineer.
partExplanations.z3: The data scientist produces the first working prototype.
partExplanations.z4: The ML engineer turns the prototype into a service-ready package.
partExplanations.z5: Scheduled refresh and a revert plan are MLOps life cycle automation.
partExplanations.z6: The security architect designs access controls and attack testing for the endpoint.

stem: Configure the charter and policy settings for the new AI Center of Excellence at Tidewater Mutual.

fields.label: Membership of the Center of Excellence

options.text: Data scientists and developers from one business unit
Executive sponsors and legal staff with no technical members
AI engineering, data science and information security

fields.label: Approval authority for high-impact model launches

options.text: Named approvers in the policy, with a risk owner
Whoever built the model, with no independent review
The vendor that supplied the model, by email reply

fields.label: Review cadence for the AI policy

options.text: Written once at launch and not revisited afterward
Scheduled review plus review on any new AI use
Reviewed only after a serious incident occurs
Findings stay with the project team to resolve
Findings are summarized in the staff newsletter
Findings go to senior leadership for a decision

fields.label: Handling of exceptions to the policy

options.text: Time-limited and documented, with approval under the policy
Granted verbally by any manager, with no record
Handled informally and not recorded, to save effort

explanation: A balanced membership, named approval authority, scheduled and event-driven reviews, a defined escalation path and documented time-limited exceptions give the charter and policy teeth. The rejected options narrow expertise, remove accountability or leave decisions untraceable.

partExplanations.members: The group needs engineering, analytical and security skills to judge AI projects.
partExplanations.approval: The policy names who decides, so authority is clear and independent of the builder.
partExplanations.cadence: Scheduled review keeps the policy current and new AI uses trigger an early update.
partExplanations.escalate: Unresolved high risks need a decision-maker above the project team.
partExplanations.exception: Documented, time-limited exceptions keep authority and traceability intact.

stem: Review these findings from an internal AI governance assessment. For each row, choose the role accountable for closing the gap.
